extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, metaphysics, and epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: An exposition and critique of philosophical methods (starting-points and principles) concerning subject, object, idea, and the limits of science; it prescribes how to approach the investigation of the world (phenomena) and the thing-in-itself. The text contrasts materialism, Fichtean subjectivism, and the author's own method based on the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between perception, understanding, and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception (immediate idea) is distinct from the understanding and from reason; perceptual illusions remain despite abstract explanations of reason, because perception 'belongs to the understanding alone' and is not corrected by reason's abstract knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the moon appears larger at the horizon than at the zenith — this illusion cannot be dispelled by reason's explanation about atmosphere; reason 'can only prevent error ... by opposing to it a truth' but cannot remove perceptual appearances. Treat perceptual data and abstract reasoning as separate faculties when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start philosophical method from the idea (not from subject or object)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin from the idea, which 'contains and presupposes' both subject and object; the antithesis of subject and object is the primary universal form of the idea, and so the idea is the correct starting-point for philosophical method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with traditional systems that start from the object or from the subject and attempt to explain the other from it; starting from the idea avoids the reciprocal fallacies of those approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict the principle of sufficient reason to the object/phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of sufficient reason is valid only in the sphere of phenomena (the object) and not with respect to the relation of subject and object; it is 'relative and conditioned' rather than an unconditioned 'veritas aeterna.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply the principle of sufficient reason uncritically to metaphysical questions about the thing-in-itself or to the subject–object relation; this misapplication leads to dogmatic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deriving the subject from the object (materialism) or the object from the subject (Fichte) as absolute starting-points
rubrics_metrics.description: Both extremes—materialism (starting from matter/object) and Fichtean subjectivism (starting from the ego/subject)—commit the same fundamental fallacy of assuming what they seek to deduce; materialism treats matter as absolutely existing and disregards the subject, while Fichte treats the ego as the unconditioned ground of the non-ego.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for petitio principii: if a system presupposes the existence/primacy of the thing it intends to explain, its deductions are circular. The proper method avoids privileging subject or object as the absolute ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: No object without a subject (principle for evaluating ontological claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: All objective reality (the world as idea) is presented only through the forms of knowledge (space, time, causality) and thus depends on the knowing subject; 'no object without a subject' — talk of suns and planets without an eye that sees them is meaningless for the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing ontological or scientific claims about 'independent' objects, account for the role of the subject and the forms of knowledge that constitute the object's presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every science must have two principal data: an organon and a special object
rubrics_metrics.description: Each science starts from two data: (1) the principle of sufficient reason in some form as organon and (2) its special object as problem (e.g., geometry: space; arithmetic: time; natural science: matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate or construct a systematic science, identify its organon (governing principle) and its special object. Examples provided: geometry (space + organon), arithmetic (time + organon), logic (combination of concepts + ground of knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify philosophical systems by their class of possible objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical systems that start from the object divide according to four classes of possible objects: (1) the real world (materialists, Epicurus, Democritus), (2) the abstract conception (Spinoza, Eleatics), (3) time/number (Pythagoreans, Y-King), and (4) the act of will directed by knowledge (schoolmen/creationism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification as a heuristic to identify what a system takes as its primary object and to reveal consequent limitations or biases in its explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science cannot give a complete explanation of the inmost nature of the world (limits of natural science)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural science, governed by causality and the principle of sufficient reason, can never reach the thing-in-itself or give a final, adequate explanation of the world's inmost nature because it is confined to relations among ideas/phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating scientific claims about 'ultimate' explanations, recognize the methodological limit: science explains relations among phenomena but not the thing-in-itself; avoid elevating causal explanation to metaphysical completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek the thing-in-itself outside the categories/forms of idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The inner nature of the world (the thing-in-itself) is not to be found in subject or object as forms of the idea but must be sought in something 'quite different and quite distinct from the idea' (to be explored as 'will' in the following book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to locate the kernel of reality within the relational/phenomenal forms (space, time, causality); methodological investigations of the thing-in-itself require a different approach than those adequate for phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: The understanding's proper function: immediate knowledge of causal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The understanding has one function only: the immediate knowledge of the relation of cause and effect; common sense, sagacity, and inventiveness are manifestations of this single function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing cognitive faculties or theories of knowledge, treat the understanding as principally the faculty for causal ordering; other faculties (reason, perception) have distinct roles that must not be conflated with understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual virtue: pursue truth and root out error regardless of immediate utility
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to follow truth even when no utility is apparent and be anxious to discover and eradicate error, for 'all error has poison at its heart' and its harm may be indirect and unforeseen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value truth-seeking as an intrinsic intellectual duty; when evaluating ideas or practices, prefer the slow, laborious triumph of truth over the temporary reign of error—truth, once fully and distinctly expressed, is not permanently vanquished.
